If you would like to use _Hash-Checking Mode_ available in `pip` since
version 8.0, `pip-compile` offers `--generate-hashes` flag:

facts.span: resolver_cls = LegacyResolver if resolver_name == "legacy" else BacktrackingResolver

pip-tools.q: Which pip-tools requirement files should be version-controlled, and what does the newline helper return if its strategy remains preserve after checking input files?

facts.span:
Generally, yes. If you want a reproducible environment installation available
from your source control, then yes, you should commit both `requirements.in`
and `requirements.txt` to source control.
facts.description: Commit both requirements.in and requirements.txt for reproducible installation.
The preserve fallback returns the LF newline string.

flask.q: Which Flask installation extra enables coroutine error handlers, and does registering a handler automatically set the response's HTTP status?

facts.span:
Routes, error handlers, before request, after request, and teardown
functions can all be coroutine functions if Flask is installed with the
``async`` extra (``pip install flask[async]``).
facts.description: The flask[async] extra enables coroutine views, error handlers, and request hooks.

facts.span:
The status code of the response will not be set to the handler's code. Make
sure to provide the appropriate HTTP status code when returning a response from
a handler.
facts.description: A handler must explicitly return the appropriate status code.

flask.q: Does a Flask async view free its worker to handle other requests, and how is an exception handler selected if there are code and class registrations?

facts.span: Each request still ties up one worker, even for async views.
facts.description: An async Flask request still occupies one worker.

facts.span:
When Flask catches an exception while handling a request, it is first looked up by code.
If no handler is registered for the code, Flask looks up the error by its class hierarchy; the most specific handler is chosen.
facts.description: Flask first checks the HTTP code, then chooses the most specific registered class handler.

facts.span: The original error is available as ``e.original_exception``.
facts.description: The wrapped original exception is available through e.original_exception.

flask.q: How can a Flask extension decorator support coroutine views, and why can't a blueprint's handler catch a routing-level 404?

facts.span:
Extension authors can support async functions by utilising the
:meth:`flask.Flask.ensure_sync` method.
facts.description: Extension authors can wrap view calls using Flask.ensure_sync.

facts.span:
the blueprint cannot handle 404 routing errors
because the 404 occurs at the routing level before the blueprint can be
determined.
facts.description: Routing 404s happen before Flask can determine the blueprint, so its handler cannot handle them.

flask.q: Which framework do Flask's docs suggest considering for a mainly async codebase, and what replaces a registered 500 handler in debug mode?

facts.span:
If you have a mainly async codebase it
would make sense to consider `Quart`_.
facts.description: Flask's docs suggest Quart for a mainly asynchronous codebase.

facts.span:
In debug mode, a handler
for "500 Internal Server Error" will not be used. Instead, the
interactive debugger will be shown.
facts.description: Debug mode shows the interactive debugger rather than using the 500 error handler.
